name: Vitamin C for gums
lead: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is used or proposed for gum health and gum appearance in two ways: as a dietary nutrient whose deficiency causes bleeding, swollen gums, and in recent dental trials as a topical or injected agent for lightening dark gum pigmentation [1][2][3]. People look to it for healthier-looking pink gums, less bleeding and, in the dental setting, a more even gum colour in the smile.

Vitamin C is a cofactor for the enzymes that hydroxylate proline and lysine in collagen, which lets collagen form its triple helix and supports blood vessels and connective tissue [4]. Scurvy, caused by inadequate vitamin C, includes gum disease and loosening teeth among its signs, and the gum changes resolve when vitamin C is restored [1][4].

Beyond scurvy, general reference sources do not establish an effect on ordinary gum disease. Several registered trials have studied vitamin C applied by microneedling, injection or mesotherapy to treat dark gum pigmentation [2][3][5][6].

chain: Vitamin C supports collagen and blood-vessel integrity in gum tissue
Deficiency-related bleeding and swelling resolve when intake is restored
In dental trials, applied vitamin C is tested for lightening dark gum pigment
angle.text: For people with low intake, restoring vitamin C reverses the bleeding and swollen gums of scurvy, which affects how gums look. Dental researchers are also testing vitamin C delivered by microneedling, injection or mesotherapy to even out darker gum pigmentation.

infobox: Dietary supplement; investigational in dental procedures

paras: Scurvy gum changes resolve with vitamin C treatment, and symptoms usually take at least a month of little or no intake to appear [1]. Historical accounts describe gum overgrowth in sailors [1]. Wikipedia's vitamin C article lists bleeding gums among later signs of deficiency, with tooth loss in advanced scurvy, after early signs such as malaise, lethargy and easy bruising [4].

Fruits and vegetables are the richest sources; Wikipedia lists acerola at about 1,677 mg per 100 g, kiwifruit and broccoli at about 90 mg and orange or lemon at about 53 mg, noting that animal foods contribute little and heat destroys much of the vitamin [4]. The US recommended dietary allowance is 90 mg per day for adult men and 75 mg for adult women, with about 35 mg more estimated for smokers [4]. The US tolerable upper intake level is 2,000 mg per day, set because gastrointestinal effects were reported above 3,000 mg [4].

Dark gum pigmentation from melanin is a cosmetic concern, and dental trials compare vitamin C delivered by microneedling, injection or mesotherapy with other approaches such as diode laser [2][3][5][6]. One trial examines vitamin C as an adjunct for pigment recurrence [7], and another registered study will test liquid nitrogen with ascorbic acid [8]. Results were not found for most of these.

Wikipedia's vitamin C article says large doses may cause gastrointestinal discomfort, headache, trouble sleeping and flushing [4]. The dental techniques used in the registered trials are investigational; the registrations used here do not report adverse-event results.

Registered studies include a completed trial of vitamin C mesotherapy versus diode laser for physiologic gingival pigmentation (n=26, started 2022) [3]; a trial of microneedling with vitamin C versus injectable vitamin C (n=22, status unknown) [5]; a phase 4 trial of vitamin C and pigment recurrence (n=24) [7]; a recruiting study of vitamin C for gingival depigmentation (n=30) [2]; a phase 2 study pairing vitamin C with glutathione (n=30) [9]; and a not-yet-recruiting phase 1/2 microneedling study (n=30) [6]. Results from these were not available.

A registered trial also explores vitamin C and orthodontic relapse (n=36) [10]. Two further registered trials test vitamin C chewing gum for nausea in pregnancy; they concern nausea rather than gum health [11][12].

On T Nation, vitamin C appears in passing in supplement lists and nutrition logs. One poster listed soft inflamed gums and a bad taste in the mouth among the signs of vitamin C deficiency he had experienced himself [13]. Another poster argued that absorption falls at doses above 1 g per day, so a 2,000 mg supplement would mostly be excreted [14].

timeline.event: James Lind trial showed citrus fruit could treat scurvy [1].
Link between hexuronic acid and scurvy established; later named ascorbic acid [1].

lore.intro: Vitamin C comes up on training forums mainly as a general supplement and as a sign-of-deficiency question [13][14].

claims.claim: Soft, inflamed gums can signal vitamin C deficiency
claims.believers: A T Nation poster described soft inflamed gums, bad taste in the mouth and tooth ache as deficiency symptoms he had personally experienced [13].
claims.experts: Wikipedia's scurvy article lists gum disease and loosening teeth among signs of severe deficiency, which takes at least a month of little or no intake to appear [1].

claims.claim: High-dose vitamin C supplements are largely excreted
claims.believers: A T Nation poster wrote that absorption drops above 1 g per day and unmetabolised vitamin C is excreted in urine [14].
claims.experts: The US tolerable upper intake level is 2,000 mg per day, set because gastrointestinal effects appeared above 3,000 mg [4].

card.summary: Vitamin C reverses scurvy gum bleeding; dental trials of gum depigmentation are ongoing with little published.
card.note: Benefit shown for deficiency; effects in healthy gums are not established.

quick.overview:
Vitamin C is needed to make collagen, and severe deficiency (scurvy) causes bleeding, swollen gums and loose teeth. Those signs resolve when vitamin C is restored.

In dentistry, small registered trials test vitamin C applied to lighten dark gum pigmentation.
quick.mechanism: Vitamin C supports collagen formation, which maintains blood vessels and connective tissue.
quick.risks: Dietary vitamin C is generally well tolerated. The dental techniques in trials are investigational.
